statement: With stock 13/50 gearing and the stock 120/80-19 rear tire, road speed per 1,000 rpm works out to about 1: 4.3 mph, 2: 5.3 mph, 3: 6.3 mph, 4: 7.5 mph, 5: 8.6 mph. One more tooth on the rear sprocket makes every gear about 2.0% shorter; one less on the front about 8.3% shorter.

vals.gear_1: 4.3 mph (6.9 km/h) per 1,000 rpm; overall ratio 18.36:1
vals.gear_2: 5.3 mph (8.6 km/h) per 1,000 rpm; overall ratio 14.81:1
vals.gear_3: 6.3 mph (10.2 km/h) per 1,000 rpm; overall ratio 12.46:1
vals.gear_4: 7.5 mph (12.1 km/h) per 1,000 rpm; overall ratio 10.49:1
vals.gear_5: 8.6 mph (13.9 km/h) per 1,000 rpm; overall ratio 9.18:1

notes: Worked out from Kawasaki's published primary ratio 2.727, gearbox ratios and final drive 13/50: speed = rpm / (primary x gear x final) x tire circumference. Tire rolling diameter is estimated from the size code (rim 19 in + 2 x 120 mm x 80%) = 675 mm; a knobby under load rolls slightly smaller, so real speeds run a little lower. Multiply by rpm/1,000 for a given engine speed.

vals.gear_1: 3.8 mph (6.2 km/h) per 1,000 rpm; overall ratio 20.66:1
vals.gear_2: 4.8 mph (7.8 km/h) per 1,000 rpm; overall ratio 16.43:1
vals.gear_3: 5.6 mph (9.1 km/h) per 1,000 rpm; overall ratio 14.06:1
vals.gear_4: 7.1 mph (11.3 km/h) per 1,000 rpm; overall ratio 11.25:1
vals.gear_5: 8.8 mph (14.2 km/h) per 1,000 rpm; overall ratio 9.00:1

notes: Worked out from Yamaha's published primary ratio 3.000, gearbox ratios and final drive 14/50: speed = rpm / (primary x gear x final) x tire circumference. statement: The mid-2022 KTM 250 SX-F Factory Edition was the first bike with the new engine and frame: 81 x 48.5 mm, compression up from 14.4 to 14.5:1, exhaust valves up from 26.5 to 27.5 mm, a lighter head, engine tilted 2 degrees back, 8 mm shorter engine, 3 mm lower countershaft sprocket, 22 mm rear axle (was 25 mm), new WP shock and quickshift.
notes: Magazine repeats KTM data. The article calls the old engine the '2013 engine'; the 78 x 52.3 mm engine actually ran 2016-2022 (a magazine 2022 race test says the engine premiered in 2016).

source.name: Motocross Action: MXA Race Test 2022-1/2 KTM 250SXF Factory Edition

statement: For 2023 nearly every engine part changed: bigger bore and shorter stroke allowing bigger ports, a lighter head, DOHC with DLC-coated finger followers, titanium valves (32.5 mm intake, 27.5 mm exhaust), a new 44 mm throttle body, an engine 8 mm shorter and tilted 2 degrees back, and new frame, swingarm, subframe, shock and bodywork shared with the 450.
notes: Valve sizes also in KTM 250 XC-F press text. Weight rose from 218 lb (2022) to 224-226 lb depending on scale.

statement: For 2025 the frame kept its geometry but lost material for more flex: relief holes in the forged shock tower, hollowed head stays, thinner backbone plates and thinner-wall long tubes. The linkage arms got shorter and thinner with smaller bolts (17 to 15 mm and 17 to 14 mm), shock valving got slightly stiffer with low-stiction seals, the swingarm top was lowered with a raised buffer pad, traction control was improved and the rear brake pedal tip was strengthened.
notes: 2023-2024 aftermarket linkages do not fit 2025. 2024 radiator graphics do not fit 2025 shrouds. Testers felt the softer frame most in acceleration chop. A magazine says KTM did not announce any mapping changes.

statement: All three use the same engine and ECU but breathe differently: the KTM has open vents in the subframe under the seat and an optional vented airbox cover, the Husqvarna has the vents moulded shut, and the GasGas has the most closed-off airbox cover. GasGas also has an extra baffle/restrictor in the muffler.

vals.KTM: open subframe vents, optional vented cover
vals.Husqvarna: vents moulded shut, optional vented cover

notes: A magazine says KTM deliberately limits the Husqvarna's breathing to keep the brands distinct. The closed airboxes cost throttle response more than dyno peak numbers.

topic: why it feels the way it does
statement: The short 48.5 mm a tester, light finger-follower valvetrain and big titanium valves let the engine breathe and rev to 14,000 rpm. Peak torque arrives around 9,200-9,600 rpm but peak power not until about 13,000-13,500 rpm, so power keeps rising for over 4,000 rpm after the torque peak. On the YZ250F that gap is under 2,800 rpm, which is why the Yamaha feels punchy and then signs off while the KTM feels flat but keeps pulling.
notes: Gap computed from the 2025 a tuner a tester (a magazine): KTM 13,470 - 9,210 = 4,260 rpm; YZ250F 12,880 - 10,100 = 2,780 rpm. Architecture explanation combines KTM data (finger followers, valve sizes, 14,000 rpm) with testers' descriptions; the link between them is BAK's engineering reading.

vals.arming: TC + QS buttons together at idle

notes: The 30% figure comes from a magazine describing a 2017 KTM; not confirmed for the 2023+ system. Testers rarely use launch control on dirt starts but do on concrete.

statement: Adding one tooth to the rear sprocket gives more low-rpm pull for riders who do not like to rev the engine; riders who stay high in the revs may not need it.
notes: On the 2020-2022 engine testers ran a 13-tooth countershaft (similar to +3 rear teeth) to cure sluggish turn exits. GasGas comes with one tooth more (52) than KTM.

statement: The 2023+ frame squats less under power and pitches less under braking, absorbs braking and acceleration bumps better and is very stable, but felt stiff and harsh until about 8-10 hours of riding. notes: 2025 frame cut-outs reduced the harshness in chop.

statement: The short 57.5 mm stroke and big 88 mm bore let it rev past 13,000 rpm, but each combustion event is small, so torque is low (about 26-29 lb-ft versus 34-37 for a 450) and the power arrives late; peak torque sits near 8,900 rpm and peak power at 11,400-13,400 rpm.
notes: Architecture-to-feel reasoning from bore/stroke and the measured curves (Dynojet 250i FC 350 tests; a magazine 2024 shootout). Torque comparison uses the same-magazine numbers in this file.

statement: The 2023 KTM 450 SX-F started a new generation with a new frame, a redesigned SOHC engine tilted 2 degrees back, a new swingarm, a polyamide/aluminium subframe, a new Pankl gearbox and a standard quickshifter. 2024-2027 are evolutions of that platform.
notes: Generation shared with Husqvarna FC 450 (2023+) and GasGas MC 450F from 2024 (the 2023 MC 450F kept the 2022 engine and frame).

source.name: Motocross Action: First Look 2023 KTM 450SXF/350SXF/250SXF

statement: For 2023 KTM changed nearly everything: new hydroformed chromoly frame with a forged shock mount and reworked stiffness, engine rotated 2 degrees back so the countershaft sprocket sits 3 mm lower, higher compression, new airbox, hollow die-cast swingarm, shorter and lighter WP XACT shock (15 mm shorter, about 100 g lighter), fork Hydrostops, quickshifter, and bigger die-cast footpegs moved inward.
notes: Shock length/weight from a magazine 2023 race test; footpeg size from Enduro21; rest from a magazine First Look (KTM press data).

source.name: Motocross Action: First Look 2023 KTM 450SXF/350SXF/250SXF

statement: The 2023 450 SX-F Factory Edition (released mid-season) added an Akrapovic slip-on, factory triple clamps, an orange frame, factory seat and wheels, semi-floating front disc, Hinson clutch cover, holeshot device, vented airbox cover and gold chain. Price was $12,099.
notes: A magazine bike guide listing (manufacturer data).

source.name: Vital MX bike guide: 2023 KTM 450 SX-F Factory Edition

statement: 2024 was a carry-over year: new graphics with purple accents, fork and shock valving taken from the 2023.5 Factory Edition, shock high-speed compression shim stack grown from 15 to 23 shims for finer adjustment, a better-sealed start/stop switch, and a one-piece air inlet sleeve/snorkel. MSRP $11,099.
notes: A magazine race test (magazine reporting of KTM changes); one-piece snorkel listed in a magazine 2024 FE guide.

source.name: Motocross Action: MXA Race Test 2024 KTM 450SXF

statement: The 2025 450 SX-F got the Factory Edition frame (cut-outs and thinner walls at the head tube, engine mounts and shock tower, about 300 g lighter), shorter and slimmer shock linkage arms with smaller bolts and new seals, reworked fork settings, revised shock geometry for more linkage ground clearance, a swingarm with a lowered top and thicker/machined chain slider, a new silencer, new bi-composite tank shrouds, a one-piece stiffer air inlet sleeve, a stronger rear brake pedal, a new chain guide, and Dunlop Geomax MX34 tyres.
notes: Combined from KTM model page, a magazine/Bikesales range reports and a magazine tech page (MSRP).

source.name: KTM 2025 450 SX-F model page

statement: Testers report that 2025 engine changes were mostly ECU, quickshifter, throttle-body and reliability tweaks plus a new silencer that KTM says sharpens response with the map switch and is slightly quieter; the quickshifter gained two reaction speeds.
notes: A magazine describes the changes without part-level detail; KTM page confirms silencer claim.

source.name: Motocross Action: MXA Race Test 2025 KTM 450SXF

statement: 2026 changes were minimal: a threaded radiator cap that opens with less force, a protection cap on the CPC fuel connector, new graphics, and (per a magazine) a black powder-coated frame and black seat. MSRP $11,649.
notes: A magazine First Look 2026 lists the frame colour; a magazine lists price and changes.

source.name: Dirt Rider: 2026 KTM 450 SX-F Technical Overview

statement: KTM calls the 2027 450 SX-F largely unchanged: in-mould graphics with red, re-routed wiring harness with new fixing points to reduce wear, unspecified engine updates for rideability and to meet the latest FIM/AMA sound rules, and frame wording about shock-mount, engine-mount and wall-thickness optimisation. US bikes arrive late spring 2026.
notes: The frame text may repeat the 2025 frame description rather than describe a new frame; no 2027 dyno or test data found yet.

source.name: KTM South Africa 2027 450 SX-F page

statement: A magazine reported that no 2026 Husqvarna FC 450s would be sold in the USA; dealers received 2025 models instead.
notes: Magazine reporting, not a Husqvarna statement.

statement: A magazine says map 2 is smooth off the bottom with little engine braking, turns very linear and takes off in the middle, and is exceptionally strong from about 8,500 rpm to the sign-off. It pulls harder out of corners and further on top than pre-2023 models, which were down low-to-mid.
notes: Tester descriptions, 2023 and 2024 race tests.

statement: A magazine says map 2 is smooth off the bottom with little engine braking, turns very linear and takes off in the middle, and is exceptionally strong from about 8,500 rpm to the sign-off. It pulls harder out of corners and further on top than pre-2023 models, which were down low-to-mid.
notes: Tester descriptions, 2023 and 2024 race tests.

source.name: Motocross Action: MXA Race Test 2023 KTM 450SXF

statement: A magazine describes the 2025-2026 engine as broad, linear and very manageable - tractor-like down low and very strong mid to top - usable in fifth gear or in tight second-gear turns. It ranked it the second-most exciting 450 engine after the Yamaha.

statement: The carbureted 250 SX made 49.23 hp against 46.08 for the YZ250, leading by about 2 hp at 6,000 rpm, 4 hp at 7,000 and 2.6 hp at 8,000; the YZ passes it about 8,800 rpm and the KTM falls off sharply by about 9,500.
notes: Magazine dyno, brand not stated; stock bikes. The 2022 test repeats 49.23 hp (about 3 hp over YZ250).

source.name: Motocross Action - Race test 2020 KTM 250SX two-stroke

statement: Power is strongest bottom to mid with an aggressive hit when it comes on, then little top end; the 2019-2022 engine is less explosive than 2017-2018, mostly because the airbox restricts airflow.
notes: Fix suggested: one tooth smaller rear sprocket; drill airbox cover (re-jet).

topic: TC 250 carb feel vs KTM and YZ
statement: The carbureted TC 250 is concentrated bottom-to-mid and needs more shifting; the KTM is snappier off the bottom, the YZ250 focuses mid-to-high and pulls further. Map 1 is aggressive, map 2 rolls on softer for traction.
notes: Venting the cover (1-1/4 in holes) added throttle snap; fast testers liked it, slow ones did not.

source.name: Motocross Action - Race test 2021 Husqvarna TC250 two-stroke

statement: The carbureted MC 250 hits hard from the bottom and pulls harder into the midrange than the YZ250 but signs off early, so it needs short-shifting; one tooth taller gearing (14/48) calms the bottom and spreads the gears.

topic: TC 250 TBI map gap and curve

statement: The a tester TF 450-X is the standard version of the RC: same engine, mapping, chassis and KYB settings, but with a new higher-capacity Exedy clutch hub, new Belleville spring, new gearbox selector star and revised engine mounts. statement: The enduro 250 pulls with more midrange than expected and revs to about 12,500 rpm; the 450-E lugs well with a broad torque spread (third gear most of the day), pulls harder in the midrange than a typical trail bike, reaches about 100 mph in sixth, but has an abrupt rev limiter that buzzes the pegs and bars.
notes: 250 details from Enduro21 test. Why: about 30% more crank inertia and enduro cams vs MX engine.

statement: On tight, greasy woods trails the TF 450-C had little bottom end, so it needed revs and momentum; the midrange was its strength, with an ultra-linear, connected roll-on.
notes: Single test in wet West Virginia clay.

source.name: Cycle News: 2026 Triumph TF 450-C Review

topic: MX Tune Pro app and Wi-Fi module
statement: Triumph's MX Tune Pro app connects to the ECU through an accessory Wi-Fi module and loads one of 10 factory maps into Map 2 (OE, Novice, Intermediate, Expert, Hard Pack Dry/Wet, Loam Dry/Wet, Sand Dry/Wet); Map 1 always stays full power. statement: All models have an upshift quickshifter (2nd to 5th on MX/XC, 2nd to 6th on E) that cuts ignition when the lever is lifted. Opinions split: some rate it best in class and it helps the stiff gearbox; others found the ignition cut distracting, that it disengages if the lever isn't fully lifted, or that it hesitates at full throttle, so some turn it off after the start.
notes: Sources: a magazine, a magazine, a magazine RC/X, a magazine 2026 shootout (best in class), a magazine 450-E (better than KTM), MX1Onboard (irregular), a magazine Test (light pressure can upshift unexpectedly).

topic: power valve calibration after top-end work
statement: The electronic power valve must be re-taught its end stops after the cylinder is removed: plug in the brand's wake-up dongle with throttle held at half for 10 seconds, then release so the valve cycles. Skipping it can make the bike bog or not rev.
notes: Procedure as described by a magazine from dealer practice; each brand (KTM/Husqvarna/GasGas) uses its own dongle.

statement: The carbureted KTM 250 power valve starts opening at about 5,600 rpm with stock preload and is fully open at about 7,900 rpm with the stock yellow inner spring. Each full turn of the preload screw moves the opening point about 150 rpm.
notes: A magazine figures; a magazine Magazine gives identical numbers. Article covers KTM 250SX/300 (carbureted, pre-2023); mechanical design shared by Husqvarna and GasGas 250s. Likely the same figures are reprinted from KTM's own guidance.

topic: power valve preload screw - direction and feel
statement: Turning the preload screw clockwise (in) gives smoother power and broader bottom end; counterclockwise (out) gives more hit and maximum top end. Adjust in 1/8 turns; total range is six turns.
notes: CONFLICT on direction: a magazine 'This much we know' and a magazine say one turn out opens the valve 150 rpm sooner (smoother) and in opens later (more hit), the opposite of a magazine Ask the MXperts text. See conflicts. Do not loosen the two screws holding the brass adjuster body.

notes: Forum reports, 2020.

statement: Stock TBI mapping is conservative and runs flat into the rev limiter; a tuner remap kept the easy bottom end, added throttle response and mid-to-top pull, and reduced limiter hits. Pipe-specific maps exist (FMF, a tuner, DR.D).
notes: No dyno numbers published. A tester (2023 300SX) described stock as rich and lethargic and the remap as adding low-rpm response and 2nd/3rd gear pull. Tuners such as WMR and Jamie Ellis cracked the locked ECU.

statement: The YZ250 power valve is driven by a crank-gear centrifugal governor and has three pieces: a center valve that opens in the first half of control-rod rotation and two side valves that open in the second half, held by torsion springs that default it closed.
notes: Description from US patent 9,797,275 (aftermarket inventor describing the stock 1999-on design). The patent attributes the YZ250's mid-rpm 'hit' to the center valve reaching its stop, where friction and spring force cause hesitation then surge.

statement: Yamaha softened the YZ250X by raising head volume from 21.5 to 23.6 cc (compression 8.9 to 7.9:1), raising the exhaust port 0.5 mm with a matching valve shape, retarding the CDI in the mid-to-high range, and setting the governor spring/preload to open the valve sooner; the pipe is 35 mm narrower.
notes: Yamaha changes as reported by a magazine. Result: milder hit, tractable to 6,500 rpm, dip at 7,000 picking up at 7,400, same peak around 8,800 rpm, more over-rev. A real-world example of how head volume, port height, ignition and PV timing move a two-stroke's power.

notes: Yamaha changes as reported by a magazine. Result: milder hit, tractable to 6,500 rpm, dip at 7,000 picking up at 7,400, same peak around 8,800 rpm, more over-rev. A real-world example of how head volume, port height, ignition and PV timing move a two-stroke's power.

statement: A port open for a fixed number of crank degrees is open for less time as rpm rises: time = degrees / (6 x rpm). A 190-degree exhaust port is open 3.7 ms at 8,600 rpm but 7.9 ms at 4,000 rpm, which is why a tall port suits high rpm and wastes charge at low rpm.
notes: t = theta/(6N): 190/(6*8600) = 0.00368 s; 190/(6*4000) = 0.00792 s. Formula from Jennings 1964. 190 deg is an illustrative duration, not a measured figure for any bike here.

topic: principle - raise vs widen the exhaust port
statement: Raising the exhaust port opens it earlier, adding duration and time-area: peak power moves up the rpm range but the band narrows and bottom end is lost. Widening adds area without adding duration, so it gains top end while keeping the band broader.
notes: Jennings via summary; dt125r tuner thread (Calum) also notes raising the barrel lowers trapped compression and changes every port's timing, so it needs head and ignition rework. Yamaha's YZ250X (+0.5 mm exhaust plus lower compression) gains over-rev and loses hit.

statement: Blowdown is the crank angle between the exhaust opening and the transfers opening; it lets cylinder pressure fall before fresh charge enters. Because port timings are symmetric about BDC, exhaust duration = transfer duration + 2 x blowdown.

vals.example: exhaust 90 deg ATDC, transfers 115 deg ATDC = 25 deg blowdown

notes: Identity follows from symmetric piston-port timing. owners table (moped-oriented) suggests about 19 deg blowdown at 6,000 rpm rising to 32 deg at 10,000; KDX200 example: exhaust 188, transfers 126, blowdown 32 deg. Treat the rpm table as rough guidance, not MX data.

notes: Identity follows from symmetric piston-port timing. owners table (moped-oriented) suggests about 19 deg blowdown at 6,000 rpm rising to 32 deg at 10,000; KDX200 example: exhaust 188, transfers 126, blowdown 32 deg. Treat the rpm table as rough guidance, not MX data.

source.name: Marty's Garage - Two-stroke port duration reference

topic: principle - what a power valve does
statement: A fixed exhaust port height only works over a narrow rpm range. The power valve lowers the effective port top at low rpm (shorter duration, more trapped compression, pipe working better) and raises it at high rpm (more duration and time-area), widening the usable band.
notes: Yamaha's SAE paper 810922 (1981) says varying exhaust timing with speed raised output by improving delivery ratio and trapping efficiency. Historical YPVS example (RD350 street bike): about 180 deg closed below 6,000 rpm to 200 deg fully open by 8,000 rpm (rd350lc.net, citing the service manual).

notes: Speed of sound proportional to sqrt(T_abs): sqrt(873/773) = 1.063. owners lists heat wrap, smaller stinger and later ignition as ways to raise temperature and water injection as lowering it.

source.name: Moped Army wiki - Expansion chamber

statement: Header holds wave energy during blowdown; the diffuser (about 6-12 degrees) makes the suction wave; the belly diameter trades scavenging suction against port-plugging; the baffle cone makes the plugging wave; the stinger's inside diameter sets chamber pressure. Gentler cones broaden the band but lower the peak.
notes: Matches a magazine YZ250 pipe test: different shapes on the same engine moved gains between 7,000 and 9,000 rpm by up to 3 hp either way.

notes: Matches a magazine YZ250 pipe test: different shapes on the same engine moved gains between 7,000 and 9,000 rpm by up to 3 hp either way.

notes: Forum author owners (KDXRider). VHM uses 0.9 mm on the KTM 125 and 1.0 mm on the YZ125, but 1.6 mm (250) and 1.9 mm (300) on larger bores.

statement: On the VHM 250 TBI head, going from the 22.6 cc to the 21.4 cc insert raises full-stroke compression by roughly 0.6 of a ratio point, which is why the smaller insert calls for 105 RON fuel.
notes: CR = (249 + Vc)/Vc: (249+21.4)/21.4 = 12.64; (249+22.6)/22.6 = 12.02. Assumes VHM insert volume is the whole clearance volume, which it may not be (squish gap and gasket not included), so absolute ratios are indicative only. Trapped (exhaust-closed) compression is much lower and needs port height, which is unpublished.

statement: The 250s are undersquare (66.4/72 = 0.92), the 300 is square (1.00) and the 125s are near square (0.99). At their measured peaks, all run about 20.4-20.9 m/s mean piston speed: 250SX 20.6 m/s at 8,600, YZ250 20.9 at 8,700, 300SX 20.4 at 8,500, KTM 125 20.3 at 11,200, YZ125 20.5 at 11,300 rpm.
notes: Mean piston speed = 2 x stroke(mm) x rpm / 60000. Peak rpm from a magazine dynos (2024 250SX, 2013 YZ250, 2023 300SX, 2021 KTM 125SX, 2022 YZ125). Similar piston speeds at peak suggest both brands tune ports/pipes to similar gas-flow limits; the 125s peak higher purely because of their shorter stroke.

notes: A magazine credits the YZ125's quick-revving midrange feel to low flywheel effect.

topic: principle - ignition timing and power valve on feel (Yamaha example)
statement: Yamaha's own softening recipe for the YZ250X combines mid-to-high rpm ignition retard, earlier power-valve opening and lower compression; the result is a milder hit and broader pull with the same peak, showing how these three levers interact.
notes: Interpretation of Yamaha's documented changes; see 2t record on YZ250 vs YZ250X.

source.name: Motocross Action - Ask the MXperts: the X factor versus the non-X factor

topic: Power Tuner app: what it is and how it talks to the bike
statement: The Power Tuner app is free for iOS and Android and connects wirelessly (Wi-Fi from the bike's Communication Control Unit, CCU) to the bike's CAN-bus. It adjusts air/fuel mixture and ignition timing, sets traction and launch control, runs a lap timer, keeps a race log and shows diagnostics, maintenance and engine run time.

vals.link: Wi-Fi to on-bike CCU, CAN-bus network

notes: Yamaha US 2025 YZ450F page. CCU named on Yamaha's Power Tuner page (placement of CCU affects signal). WR models in the US need a GYTR CCU accessory (see GYTR records).

source.name: Yamaha Motor USA, 2025 YZ450F features page

It adjusts air/fuel mixture and ignition timing, sets traction and launch control, runs a lap timer, keeps a race log and shows diagnostics, maintenance and engine run time.

vals.link: Wi-Fi to on-bike CCU, CAN-bus network

notes: Yamaha US 2025 YZ450F page. CCU named on Yamaha's Power Tuner page (placement of CCU affects signal). WR models in the US need a GYTR CCU accessory (see GYTR records).

source.name: Yamaha Motor USA, 2025 YZ450F features page

statement: To connect, the bike's CCU must be powered (owners report pressing the start button), then join the bike's Wi-Fi network on the phone using the password printed on the CCU label, and accept the 'no internet' warning. The label is reached by removing the left side panel/number plate and pulling out the Wi-Fi box.

vals.password_location: label on CCU (Wi-Fi box) behind left side panel / left number plate

notes: Owner reports 2018-2024. A magazine 2023 YZ250F race test independently describes the password under the serial number on the Wi-Fi box behind the left side panel. Fixes reported: allow app local-network permission, allow networks without internet, try another phone, on iPhone set a manual IP; a missing CCU means no network.

statement: A magazine procedure: connect to the bike's Wi-Fi, open Map List in the app, add a new map, type in the fuel and ignition grids, then send it to the bike with the up-arrow button. A magazine found the process harder than it should be.
notes: Magazine procedure description, 2023 YZ250F.

notes: Listing text applies to the current app (2026). Grid breakpoints for 2023+ bikes are not stated by Yamaha; see the throttle-axis and breakpoint records.

statement: A tester map that adds low-end excitement to fill the gap before the strong mid-range hit, smoothing the bottom-to-mid transition and helping second-gear mid-range roll-on without the bike running away 50-100 ft out of a corner.
notes: Map values in image only.

source.name: Keefer Inc. Tested, 2023 Yamaha YZ450F Optional Power Tuner Maps

statement: A magazine answer to the 450's barky low end is a map that adds fuel between 2,000 and 5,000 rpm to take away crispness off idle; Yamaha's optional Smooth Linear map did not tame the low end enough for a magazine. A magazine pairs it with a 48-tooth rear sprocket (stock 49).
notes: Same richer-low-rpm approach in a magazine March 2023 race test. A magazine says it tested three maps on the 2025 YZ450F and was not satisfied with any yet (Aug 2024). Chart image URL could not be fetched.

statement: A magazine published two fuel/ignition map pairs for the 2023 YZ250F: one for smoother, broader power and one for aggressive, quick power. Mapping reduced but did not remove a jerky hesitation at the crack of the throttle in slow rutted corners.

source.name: Motocross Action, Race Test: 2023 Yamaha YZ250F

statement: A Yamaha R&D map that adds pulling power when shifting through second, third and fourth gears.
notes: Stated for 2022-2023 YZ250F (same engine).

source.name: Keefer Inc. Tested, 2023 Yamaha YZ250F Optional Yamaha Power Tuner Maps

statement: A tester map with less engine braking and a more balanced chassis feel off the throttle; owners of 2024 bikes report it adds bottom and top and is very similar to a tester map.
notes: 2024 owner comments from a magazine forum (COMMUNITY).

topic: 'a tester' map by Yamaha test rider (2024 YZ250F)
statement: Yamaha test rider Steve Tokarski's map cleans up the rich feel at low rpm and adds excitement from the crack of the throttle into the low-mid; it was run with traction control off.
notes: Owners say it is very similar to a tester Free Feeling with slightly more engine braking (a magazine forum, Nov 2023).

source.name: PulpMX, Ten things about the 2024 Yamaha YZ250F on track

statement: Owners report the 2024 YZ250F stock map has less bottom and more mid/top than 2022; the 'Responsive' map gets the low end back but hits harder; 'a tester' and 'a tester Free Feeling' add bottom and top.
notes: Small number of owners; no values.

source.name: Vital MX forum, 2024 YZ 250F Review thread

topic: A tester 2026 YZ450F map (less engine braking)
statement: The tester found the 2026 YZ450F has more engine braking than 2024-2025, making it hard to roll corners and upsetting the chassis; his map relaxes the engine on deceleration to fix corner-entry balance.

source.name: Keefer Inc. Tested, 2026 Yamaha YZ450F Optional Yamaha Power Tuner Map

topic: A tuner / Jamie Ellis map (2024 YZ450F)
statement: A magazine test bike ran a map from Jamie Ellis of a tuner to make the 450 manageable for average riders, noting the throttle-opening (TH%) settings on the vertical axis make a big difference.
notes: A magazine says the 450 needs detuning, not hot-rodding, for most riders; biggest power gain 7,500-10,000 rpm.

source.name: Dirt Bike, Riding the 2024 Yamaha YZ450F long term: the wrap

topic: YZ450FX tester maps (Magic Map, JL Smooth)
statement: On the 2023 YZ450FX, Yamaha's 'Magic Map' softened the initial hit while keeping pull (some said it revved like a 350) and suited motocross and fast terrain but was abrupt in tight, low-traction ground; the tester-made 'JL Smooth' map was preferred for tight terrain and let riders lug it with little clutch.

source.name: Dirt Bike Test, 2023 Yamaha YZ450FX test

topic: YZ450FX maps and traction control in mud
statement: On the 2024 YZ450FX the tester ran the mellow map 2 most of the day in muddy, tight terrain, softened both maps further and added traction control through the app.
notes: TC level not stated.

source.name: Dirt Bike Test, 2024 Yamaha YZ450FX off-road racer first impression

statement: Testers preferred the standard map on the 2025 YZ250F; the performance map adds mid and top but takes away too much bottom in places.

source.name: Dirt Bike Test, 2025 Yamaha YZ250F first impression

statement: An owner set every cell to -10 fuel and -10 ignition on a 2023 YZ450F; the rpm built more slowly and power dropped, making the bike feel like a 350 on one map and a full 450 on the other.
notes: Single owner video. Note: in this app minus fuel is leaner, which normally sharpens response; the owner's result is reported as-is.

source.name: YouTube, mxengineer1: 2023 YZ450F turned into YZ350F with Yamaha Power Tuner

topic: What fuel and ignition changes do to the feel (Yamaha test rider guidance)
statement: More fuel gives a smoother response and slower rpm rise; less fuel gives quicker response and faster rpm rise. More ignition advance sharpens response and adds a little perceived power; retard softens it. More fuel plus more advance gives slower revving with a stronger torque feel.
notes: Change one region at a time and switch back to the other map to confirm the feel.

topic: Dyno effect of Power Tuner maps (2024 YZ450F)
statement: On a Dyno Dynamics dyno the stock 2024 YZ450F made 56.4 hp at 9,500 rpm; about two hours of leaner fuel and more advance gained only 0.6 hp with more torque across most of the range (too much advance made it too aggressive to ride), while maximum fuel and maximum retard cut peak to 51.4 hp with a much gentler, slower-revving feel that still revved past 11,000 rpm.
notes: Dyno Tech (Melbourne), Dyno Dynamics dyno; stock exhaust and air filter; fuel not stated. Article notes US Dynojets usually read higher. Tuned peak is DERIVED (56.4 + 0.6).

source.name: Australasian Dirt Bike, 2024 Yamaha YZ450F dyno test

topic: Yamaha's WR mapping ideas (soft / medium / aggressive)
statement: Yamaha Australia's WR guide: a Soft map adds fuel at low rpm and retards ignition (with higher traction control) for beginners and slippery or technical trails; Medium adjusts fuel through the midrange for drive; Aggressive leans slightly and advances ignition with TC off for open terrain and experienced riders. Testers liked Medium best on the WR450F.

vals.soft: +fuel low rpm, ignition retarded, TC higher
vals.medium: midrange fuel tuned, ignition softened in key areas
vals.aggressive: slightly leaner, advanced ignition, TC off

notes: Qualitative only. Applies to WR but the fuel/ignition logic carries over to YZ.

statement: For 2025 Yamaha revised the rear linkage and shock settings, updated fork settings (delta-shaped piston shims), changed the front engine mounts, increased clutch-plate oil holes from 6 to 18, added a raised-rib handlebar switchbox, and fitted lighter aluminum footpeg brackets.

source.name: Yamaha Motor USA 2025 YZ450F features page

statement: Testers report the 2025 front engine mounts went back to a single piece after two years of two thinner pieces, the throttle tube was moved out 10 mm to reduce blisters, and the MSRP stayed $9,999.
notes: A magazine describes the 2025 linkage as stiffer and the spring rate softer, with new ECU map settings (mxa25v). Yamaha's 2025 US spec page later showed $10,299 MSRP; a magazine reported $9,999 at launch.

source.name: Cycle News, 2025 Yamaha YZ450F review

statement: 2026 brought a redesigned intake port (stronger tumble, more linear low-mid response), new intake and exhaust resonators for noise rules, a new frame with a thinner front downtube, a new KYB shock with hand-adjustable low-speed compression, revised fork settings, a standard hydraulic clutch with new inner hub, and a password ECU lock in the Power Tuner app.
notes: A magazine lists the hydraulic clutch under the YZ250F section, but the a magazine text (a magazine) and Yamaha Australia (MCNews) confirm it for the YZ450F.

source.name: GateDrop, 2026 YZ450F revealed (Yamaha USA release)

statement: A magazine reports the 2026 engine also got a new cam, flywheel inertia up 8%, a head-pipe resonator and new muffler; clutch spring tension up 10%; and stock rear sprocket changed from 49 to 51 teeth. Frame: more lateral rigidity at the forged downtube, softer engine cradle, changed engine hangers, top shock mount less vertically rigid; geometry unchanged.
notes: Magazine-reported technical briefing details; not found in Yamaha USA public spec pages.

source.name: Dirt Bike Magazine, 2026 Yamaha YZ450F full test

statement: Australian launch info lists 2026 shock main-valve ports up from 4 to 6, base valve piston enlarged from 24 mm to 28 mm with two-way oil passages, a piston cooler, a new magneto, front engine mount thickness 6 mm and asymmetric rear engine mounts.
notes: BikeReview's spec table also says 'cable clutch actuation' while its text describes the hydraulic clutch; spec table appears copied from an older sheet.

source.name: BikeReview.com.au, 2026 YZ450F launch test

statement: The 2027 YZ450F is announced (June 2026) at $10,299 ($10,499 Monster Energy Edition). The only change found is a new rear brake: smaller caliper, smaller master-cylinder piston and a 220 mm rear disc (was 240 mm), claimed 180 g lighter.
notes: 220 mm rear disc and 109 kg wet from Yamaha Australia 2027 spec sheet; caliper/master cylinder and 180 g claim from Yamaha copy on a US dealer listing (at27); prices from Motorcycle & Powersports News (mpn27). No engine change was published.

statement: Worked out from Yamaha's 60.8 mm stroke, mean piston speed is about 23.7 m/s at the 11,700 rpm limiter and about 19.9 m/s at the 9,800 rpm power peak.

notes: magazine testers: front traction in flat turns and ruts weaker than Honda/KTM (vital26). A tester: one of the most stable, not as good as 2022 (kif26w).

statement: Stock triple clamp offset is 22 mm; magazine testers preferred 23 mm aftermarket clamps for stability.

statement: 2026 shock gets a new base valve and a hand-adjustable low-speed compression clicker for smoother low-to-high-speed transition; testers call the setup stiff but well balanced, best at high speed on rough tracks.
notes: Valve detail in br26 (4->6 ports, 24->28 mm base valve).

source.name: GateDrop, 2026 YZ450F revealed (Yamaha USA release)

statement: 2025 revised linkage (a magazine: stiffer linkage, softer spring) and fork shims; Yamaha suggests 106 mm sag per a magazine.
notes: Linkage ratio numbers not published.

source.name: Yamaha Motor USA 2025 YZ450F features page

statement: A magazine 2023 setup: fork 5.0 N/mm springs, 270 cc oil, compression 10 out, rebound 13 out, forks flush; shock 58 N/mm, 105 mm sag (stock 100), HSC 1-1/8 turns out, LSC 12 out, rebound 13 out.
notes: Testers slid forks down in clamps to reduce head-shake.

source.name: Motocross Action, race test of the 2023 YZ450F

statement: A magazine 2024: for quicker steering about 102 mm sag and forks up 7 mm; for stability 105-108 mm sag and forks flush.

source.name: Dirt Bike Magazine, 2024 YZ450F full test

statement: 2025: a magazine ran 102 mm sag and 2 clicks softer fork; a magazine raised forks 5 mm with 103 mm sag. 2026: a magazine runs about 106 mm sag, forks flush for fast tracks, forks up about 2 mm for tight tracks.
notes: Sources: cn25, swap25, db26.

statement: Dirt can pass the thin filter-cage channel at the front, and because the backfire screen is part of the filter cage, pulling the filter lets dirt drop into the throttle body. Fix: heavy grease on the filter front edge, cover the intake when servicing.
notes: Repeated in a magazine 2024 test.

statement: The 2023-2024 disc-spring cable clutch faded early in motos and testers judged the spring too soft; fixes were a stiffer aftermarket disc spring or the GYTR hydraulic kit. Yamaha added more clutch oil holes for 2025 and a hydraulic clutch with 10% more spring tension for 2026.
notes: See mxa24, ym25f, db26.

statement: With the 51-tooth rear sprocket, 2nd gear runs out quickly and 3rd struggles in some corners; 13/50 is a common fix.
notes: magazine testers also noted more shifting (vital26).

source.name: Keefer Inc Testing, 2026 YZ450F gearing

statement: Some magazine testers found the 2026 fork overpowered the shock and turned harsh deeper in the stroke; raising the forks and softening the front helped.
notes: Other tests praised the fork; treat as setup-dependent.

notes: cn25 also notes stiff seat foam.
